complaint.title: BigWave et al. vs. POSCO Holdings
complaint.subtitle: Alleged pollution from POSCO steel mill in Indonesia
affected: BigWave et al. vs. National Pension Service
complaint.allegations:
On 19 August 2026, Big Wave, WALHI Jakarta and CELIOS filed a set of complaints against POSCO Holdings, POSCO and the National Pension Service (NPS) of Korea at the Korean NCP. The complaints concern the greenhouse gas emissions and pollution of the Krakatau POSCO coal-fired steel mill in Cilegon, Banten, Indonesia.
The complainants allege that emissions from the Krakatau POSCO mill, which is the largest carbon emitter among POSCO’s overseas facilities, cause health hazards for nearby residents. The complaints claim that PM2.5 concentration levels in nearby areas are around 18 times the WHO recommended limit and that iron dust from the mill has caused itchy skin among residents. They state that nearby villages have seen a rise in cases of acute respiratory infections from 665 to 1,065 cases in a year. The complaints further allege that the National Pension Service, despite holding around 8% of POSCO Holdings, has failed to use its leverage to address the harms.
The complainants are asking that POSCO publicly disclose measures to reduce and monitor emissions from the Krakatau POSCO mill, convert its No.1 blast furnace to a hydrogen-based facility and cease the expansion of its No.2 blast furnace expansion and announce a 2050 carbon neutrality roadmap for its overseas operations.

case.title: POSCO Daewoo's PT Bio Inti Agrindo Forest Clearing in Merauke
case.place: Ulilin, Merauke Regency, South Papua, Indonesia
case.point: PT BIA concession, Ulilin district, Merauke (approximate)

lenders.name: POSCO and Daewoo International (POSCO Daewoo) (South Korea) (foreign investor)
lenders.role: Daewoo bought 85% of PT Bio Inti Agrindo in 2011; POSCO held 60.3% of Daewoo (Norway Council on Ethics).

case.conditions: No lender is recorded. The concession covers 32,500 ha in two blocks inside the government's Merauke Integrated Food and Energy Estate (Norway Council on Ethics; EJAtlas).
case.community: Since 2012 PT BIA has cleared forest at Iltadeh, Ulilin, without the consent of the Mahuze Kewam indigenous clan who own the land, according to a 2018 report by GRAIN, the TANY Collective and the Papuan group Yayasan Pusaka. The report says the company paid one sum to people from another village who did not own the land and later made a payment and promises to the Mahuze Kewam without a contract setting the area, duration or price, and that the promises were not kept (GRAIN).
case.suppression: The GRAIN report says military officers guarding the plantation committed violent acts in 2015 and 2016, and that security officers shot towards villagers who had blocked the entrance to the plantation (GRAIN).
case.ecosystem: Norway's Council on Ethics found about 3,000 ha cleared between February and November 2014, all forest in the western block apparently removed, and about 260 fire hotspots in and near the concession from 2011 to August 2014; it judged the area mostly tropical forest, against the company's description of shrubland. EJAtlas, citing satellite mapping, puts total forest loss at 26,500 ha from 2012 to 2017.
case.outcome: On 27 March 2015 the Council on Ethics recommended excluding POSCO and Daewoo from Norway's sovereign wealth fund over an unacceptable risk of severe environmental damage (Norway Council on Ethics); the fund dropped them in August 2015 (Mongabay). Daewoo denied using fire to clear land and said fires were started by workers or local people (Norway Council on Ethics).

complaint.title: KTNC Watch et al vs. POSCO International, National Pension Service and KEXIM
complaint.subtitle: POSCO’s violations in palm plantation in Papua, Indonesia
complaint.concluded: 13 January 2022, Related complaints, KTNC Watch et al vs. National Pension Service, POSCO International and KEXIM, KTNC Watch et al vs. KEXIM, POSCO International and National Pension Service
complaint.allegations:
On 12 December 2019
KTNC
Watch
, PUSAKA, SKP-KAMe, and W
AL
HI Papua filed a specific instance against Posco Internation
al and two of its financiers, the the Export-Import Bank of Korean (KEXIM)
and the Nation
al
Pension Service (NPS) at the Korean NCP. The complaint argues that POSCO Internation
al
‘s subsidiary in the palm industry in Papua, Indonesia, has been engaged in business activities causing a range of adverse health, labour rights, and environmental impacts. The complaint alleges that POSCO as well as its financiers (lenders) failed to implement adequate human rights due diligence to identify and address the adverse impacts caused by the subsidiary.
The complainants seek the Korean NCP’s good offices to encourage
the three companies
to adopt policies for reviewing environment
al
and soci
al
risks in developing natur
al
resources overseas, and more specifically to refrain from providing further loans to support the operations of POSCO Internation
al
‘s subsidiary in Papua.
complaint.outcome:
On 17 March 2020, the Korean NCP issued an initial assessment accepting the complaint for good offices. The NCP accepted the complaint regarding POSCO and the National Pension Service. The NCP also accepted the complaint against KEXIM. The NCP clarified that in this matter, KEXIM could be considered a multinational enterprise covered by the OECD Guidelines because 1) it has oversea branches in the United Kingdom, Indonesia, and Vietnam; 2) in this case, its funding of POSCO was not related to any official development assistance projects; and 3) the financial services it provided to POSCO, providing loans and taking interest, were commercial in nature like those of a typical financial institution. The NCP also found the complaint satisfied the other Guidelines’ admissibility criteria.
On 13 January 2022, the Korean NCP published its final statement in relation to the complaints against Posco International and NPS. The NCP facilitated three mediation meetings between the parties, but they were unable to reach a full agreement on the issues raised in the complaints. However, the NCP opined that as a result of the mediation “both parties recognized the need to listen to the opinions of local people and establish a system for in-depth dialogue with local residents.” The NCP considered that Posco International had complied with the Guidelines in several respects and that NPS had taken steps to improved its ESG measures.
The NCP made recommendations to both Posco International and NPS, including:
For both Posco International and NPS to establish communication channels to deal with the issues raised by the complainants and continue their engagement;
For Posco International to explain to the complainant the company’s efforts to resolve the issues, including through consultations with local residents about the complaint, compensation, and improvement measures;
For Posco International to implement the ‘No Deforestation, No Peat, No Exploitation” (NDPE) policy and the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil (RSPO) criteria, and for both Posco International and NPS to ensure that Guidelines, the OECD Due Diligence Guidance for Responsible Business Conduct, and the Guidance for Responsible Agricultural Supply Chains are considered during the company’s due diligence process; and
For both companies to submit a performance report six months after the receipt of the final statement.

complaint.title: Leaders of Paguyuban UKPWR from the Indonesian community of Batang vs.  ITOCHU Corporation
complaint.subtitle: Human rights violations at ITOCHU & J-Power’s power plant in Indonesia
complaint.concluded: 13 February 2024, Related complaints, Leaders of Paguyuban UKPWR from the Indonesian community of Batang vs. Electric Power Development Co. Ltd.
complaint.allegations:
With the support of Greenpeace Indonesia and Friends of the Earth Japan, 23 community leaders united in Paguyuban UKPWR, on behalf of community members in Batang, Indonesia, filed complaints at the Japanese NCP against ITOCHU Corporation and Electric Power Development Co., Ltd. (‘J-Power’) for alleged harms committed by Bhimasena Power Indonesia (BPI), the joint-venture they established to construct and operate a coal-fired power plant in Batang.
Community members resist giving up their land for the construction of the project and fear the project’s impact on their income and livelihoods, agricultural land, and fishing grounds. Residents have already experienced intimidation and violence and faced, among other things, wrongful and arbitrary arrests and unfair trials.
The complainants allege that the companies have not carried out comprehensive human rights and environmental due diligence, nor engaged in meaningful consultation with all affected communities to identify the full scope and severity of potential human rights, social, and environmental impacts.
The complainants ask the NCP to help ensure that the plant’s construction process does not involve any further manipulation, coercion, intimidation, or violence towards the local community, and to help farmers and community members receive appropriate rehabilitation or remediation for the damages and negative impacts experienced. They request for the NCP to conduct an independent assessment of the case through fact-finding. The complainants hope the NCP process will lead to disclosure of important information on health and safety risks.
complaint.outcome:
On 10 September 2015, the Japanese NCP officially accepted the complaint.
On 28 June 2016, the Japanese NCP accepted the majority of the allegations raised in the complaint in its initial assessment. Aspects of the complaint concerning interpretation or enforcement of Indonesia’s laws were rejected. The NCP does not publish its initial assessment for complaints it accepts for further examination.
The long duration between the complaint being filed (July 2015), the NCP’s official acceptance of the complaint (September 2015), and the NCP’s initial assessment (June 2016) was a significant issue for the complainants. At the time the complaint was filed, the conflicts between the community (especially the landowners) and BPI needed to be resolved as soon as possible, but according to the complainants their land access was completely and forcibly shut down in March 2016 before the NCP’s conclusion of its initial assessment. This severely limited the effectiveness of the complaint, which in part sought to stop the land acquisition.
Between June 2016 and 2023, the companies refused to respond to the NCP’s offer of good offices on the basis that BPI was proceeding with its operations while communicating with the local community. During this period, the complainants did not oppose the companies’ refusals to respond, and both parties informed the NCP of developments in Indonesia.
On 19 September 2023, the Japanese NCP notified the companies that it considered them unwilling to engage in the NCP process and if no progress was made in the following two months, the NCP would terminate the complaint process and issue its final statement.
On 21 November 2023, the companies formally declined the NCP’s offer of good offices on the basis that BPI engaged with local community members through various activities and wished to continue doing so without the NCP’s involvement. On 13 February 2024, the NCP published its final statement concluding the complaint. The NCP recommended “that the Enterprises Involved continue to ensure the observance of the Guidelines and to engage with the Complainants and other members of the community, and residents, including through BPI’s initiatives.”
The complainants note that the NCP’s role is more than just to offer its good offices (mediation) for dialogue. The NCP should also proactively review companies’ compliance with the OECD Guidelines and make clear recommendations on the implementation of the Guidelines by companies.

case.title: Batang Coal Power Plant Land Takeover
case.place: Karanggeneng, Ponowareng and Ujungnegoro villages, Batang Regency, Central Java, Indonesia

lenders.name: J-Power and Itochu (Japan), through PT Bhimasena Power Indonesia
lenders.role: Two Japanese companies that, with Indonesia's Adaro Power, own the plant's developer, Bhimasena Power Indonesia (Mongabay; FoE Japan). Local leaders filed complaints against both companies with Japan's OECD contact point in July 2015 (FoE Japan).

lenders.name: Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC)
lenders.role: Agreed in June 2016 to lend about US$2,052 million and to guarantee US$1,369 million of co-financing by private banks (JBIC examiners' report); Mongabay reports a US$2.1 billion JBIC loan within a US$4 billion project funded with other Asian banks.

case.conditions: Foreign direct investment by Japanese companies in a 2,000 MW coal plant, later financed by JBIC. Land the owners would not sell was acquired under Indonesia's 2012 land procurement law, which a senior investigator at the National Human Rights Commission said was wrongly applied to a private project (Mongabay; FoE Japan).
case.community: Indonesia's National Human Rights Commission wrote in December 2015 of human rights violations in the land transfer since 2013, including intimidation and physical and mental threats against local people (FoE Japan). In March 2016 fences cut farmers off from unsold land so they could not harvest, the commission said in May 2016, and irrigation for unsold fields was destroyed by army heavy equipment clearing the site (FoE Japan); a May 2016 video showed a two-metre wall guarded by private security around 12-15 hectares that farmers said they had not sold (Mongabay). Some protesters arrested in 2013 were convicted by the Batang District Court (JBIC examiners' report). In January 2017, after work began on the jetty, fishers said a day's catch near the site had fallen to about three kilos, worth some 50,000 rupiah, against about 500,000 rupiah before (Greenpeace via Mongabay). JBIC's examiners noted photos and media footage showing several people injured during demonstrations (JBIC examiners' report).
case.suppression: Police and military were assigned to the land acquisition under a January 2013 government order (JBIC examiners' report); opponents said local security, police and the army intimidated them, and one community leader was jailed for eight months (Greenpeace via Mongabay).
case.outcome: Construction began in late 2016. JBIC's examiners found in June 2017 that JBIC had not breached its guidelines, while noting that social acceptance had not been achieved among some residents; the developer said it fenced the site in March 2016 but delayed levelling until after the June 2016 harvest and provided harvesting help, substitute farmland and 21 months of payments to tenant farmers (JBIC examiners' report).

complaint.title: Shehri-Citizens for a Better Environment vs SHV Holdings, NV
complaint.subtitle: Makro’s human rights and environment violations in Pakistan
complaint.allegations:
Shehri-Citizens for a Better Environments complaint against Dutch SHV Holdings NV alleges the company was involved in the illegal transfer and conversion of land and has committed human rights abuses and caused environmental degradation in Pakistan.
Dutch SHV Holdings NV and Pakistani House of Habib jointly owned Makro Habib Pakistan Ltd., which operates a chain of department outlet stores in Pakistan.
complaint.outcome:
The Dutch NCP accepted the case in November 2008 and forwarded it to SHV for comment. In a February 2009 meeting with the NCP, SHV denied the allegations and informed the NCP it had divested from the Makro Habib joint venture in December 2008.
After the NCP learned that a lower court in Pakistan had dismissed a similar complaint concerning the land-related issues, the complainant argued that the case was dismissed unlawfully and an appeal had been filed. In December 2009, the Supreme Court ruled in the complainant’s favour and ordered Makro-Habib to relocate.
When the NCP learned that the environmental issues had been resolved prior to the filing of the complaint, the complainant acknowledged that the issues had been remedied, but requested that the NCP determine whether the OECD Guidelines had been violated.
Once the company presented documented proof that it had fully divested from Makro Habib Pakistan Ltd. in December 2008, the NCP concluded it could no longer pursue future-oriented mediation. The NCP also decided the “investment nexus” had ceased to exist and it therefore had no basis to continue the process.

Residents of Khario Ghulam Shah, next to the mine, said dust and noise from round-the-clock excavation and trucks had become permanent, that the noise kept them awake and that respiratory illness was increasing among children and older people (T …[truncated]

complaint.title: Swiss Tibetan Friendship Association and others vs. International Olympic Committee
complaint.subtitle: International Olympic Committee’s insufficient due diligence in awarding 2022 Winter Olympics to China
complainants: Tibetan Community of Switzerland and Liechtenstein
complaint.allegations:
On 27 July 2021, Swiss Tibetan Friendship Association, Tibetan Youth Association in Europe, Tibetan Community of Switzerland and Liechtenstein, and Tibetan Women’s Association Switzerland (‘the complainants’) filed a specific instance against the International Olympic Committee (IOC) at the Swiss NCP. The complaint alleges that the IOC did not conduct sufficient due diligence and accordingly failed to avoid contributing to potential human rights and labour rights violations in Tibet, Xinjiang, Hong Kong, Inner Mongolia, and other regions in China by awarding the 2022 Winter Olympics to Beijing.
The complainants allege that the IO awarded the Winter Olympics to China despite knowing that the decision would lead to further abuses against migrant workers and people subject to forced/prison labour due to their being required to construct buildings, merchandise, and equipment for the Olympics. They also claim that several sponsors, partners, and suppliers of the Winter Olympics are (in)directly linked to the human rights and labour rights abuses in Xinjiang, China. Accordingly, the IOC is directly linked to these adverse impacts and has a responsibility under the OECD Guidelines to exercise its leverage with the Chinese government to encourage reforms.
The complainants request mediation:
To resolve the issues raised, including to identify the necessary steps to be taken by the IOC to fulfill its responsibility to respect human rights (especially of vulnerable groups) who are subject to forced/prison labour and other labour rights abuses and are engaged in activities related to the Winter Olympics.
To highlight the IOC’s responsibilities in utilizing leverage with China to encourage reforms in its policies towards vulnerable groups.
To ask the IOC to reconsider its decision to award the Winter Olympics to China if the IOC is not able to guarantee the protection of fundamental rights.
complaint.outcome:
On 23 November 2021, the Swiss NCP published its initial assessment accepting the specific instance and offering its good offices to the parties. Due to the foreseeable duration of the NCP process, the NCP suggested that mediation could focus on the mitigation and remediation of alleged adverse human rights impacts during and due to the 2022 Winter Olympics and the respect of human rights by the IOC in future Olympic Games. The NCP also suggested that mediation could contribute to consideration of the roles and responsibilities of individual actors such as sponsors and suppliers in relation to the provisions of the OECD Guidelines.
In its initial assessment, the NCP carefully considered the applicability of the OECD Guidelines to the IOC (that is, whether the IOC was a multinational enterprise (MNE) covered by the Guidelines). The NCP stated, “the key question should be whether the activities in question are of commercial nature.” In deciding that the IOC was an MNE with responsibilities under the Guidelines, the NCP referred to the IOC having “international operations and a multinational scope” and to the revenues generated from the Winter Olympics for the IOC: “Even if 90 per cent of the generated revenue is to be used to assist athletes and develop sports worldwide and only 10 per cent of the revenue are used for the operational and administrative costs of the Olympic Movement, the involvement of the IOC in the organization of the games can be considered as activities of commercial nature, to which the OECD Guidelines are applicable.” However, the NCP warned that its conclusion that the Guidelines applied to the IOC in this specific instance “does not allow the general conclusion that sports federations are multinational companies. Despite certain commercial activities according to the OECD Guidelines, the IOC and the sport federations remain non-profit organizations whose main purpose is the promotion of sport worldwide, which distinguishes it from most other multinational companies.”
On 21 December 2021, the Swiss NCP published its final statement closing the specific instance. The NCP explained that the complainants had accepted the NCP’s offer of good offices, but the IOC had not due to one of the complainants disclosing the IOC’s confidential written statement to their submission on their website. The IOC stated that the good offices process depends on good faith behaviour of all parties, including maintaining confidentiality where appropriate.
The Swiss NCP made the following recommendations to the parties before closing the specific instance:
For the IOC to maintain a dialogue with stakeholders, including the complainants.
For the IOC to disclose its policies and practices for implementing human rights due diligence regarding the awarding and holding of the Olympic Games, including its expectations towards business partners such as sponsors and suppliers having a direct link with IOC’s operations.
For the complainants to respect the rules of confidentiality in NCP processes in any future submissions to an NCP.

case.title: Houses of 86 Households Demolished and a Crane Operator Killed in the Xuancheng Industry Zone
case.place: Xuancheng Economic and Technological Development Zone, Xuanzhou district, Xuancheng city, Anhui province, China
case.point: Xuanzhou district, Xuancheng city, the district holding the Economic and Technological Development Zone whose Phase 2 the loan financed (OpenStreetMap place point for 宣州区, Xuancheng)

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Loan IBRD-82700 for the Anhui Xuancheng Infrastructure for Industry Relocation Project (P129431). US$150 million approved 20 June 2013, effective 14 November 2013; the commitment was revised to US$87,280,075 and that amount was disbursed. Original closing 30 September 2018, actual closing 31 August 2020, after two extensions. The data sheet gives the total project cost as US$343,640,000 at apprais …[truncated]

companies.name: Xuancheng Economic and Technological Development Zone Management Committee
companies.role: The zone authority, a body of the Xuancheng municipal government, which the completion report names as taking the corrective measures after the fatal accident and as running the zone's resettlement office. The zone was set up in 1996 as a 6.24 square kilometre industrial park, expanded by a further  …[truncated]

companies.name: Xuancheng project management office
companies.role: The municipal project office that managed implementation, prepared and disclosed the resettlement action plan, ran the grievance mechanism and hired the external environmental management and resettlement monitoring consultants. After the fatal accident it strengthened its safety processes and requir …[truncated]

case.conditions: The appraisal document of 20 May 2013 prints the terms as a table of two "Legal Covenants" and one "Condition" in its data sheet. The condition was one of effectiveness: the loan could not become effective until Xuancheng Municipality, through the development zone, entered into a Subsidiary Agreement with the zone's construction and investment company. The first covenant carried the date 30 June 2014: the company "shall have entered into a contract for the construction, and at least 5 years of operation and maintenance, of the wastewater treatment plant of the Project, with an entity or entities duly qualified to perform such tasks, all under terms and conditions acceptable to the Bank", cit …[truncated]
case.community: The loan paid for roads, a wastewater treatment plant and other infrastructure in the Xuancheng development zone, built so that factories moving inland from China's coast could relocate there. The resettlement action plan of 3 April 2013 had provided for the demolition of private houses of 161 households, 38,049.17 square metres in total, of which 9,719.61 square metres were brick-concrete and 23,631.98 square metres brick-wood. Because some subprojects were changed or cancelled, houses of 86 households were demolished, and a footnote to the completion report puts the area at 23,747 square metres: 'Of the planned 38,049 m2 of houses, only 23,747 m2 of houses were eventually demolished, belonging to 86 households, which received compensation as required.' The report's resettlement annex writes the same figure as a reduction - 'The total area was 23,747.06 m2 (or 38 percent) smaller than that estimated in the RAP' - which the footnote and the arithmetic of the plan figure settle as the area actually demolished. The plan had provided for permanent land acquisition of 2,558.1 mu, of which 1,676.18 mu was cultivated land; at closing 1,984.15 mu had been acquired, excluding five roads ca …[truncated]
case.outcome: The loan closed on 31 August 2020, almost two years late, with US$87.28 million of the US$150 million disbursed and the commitment cut to that amount. Lower-than-planned land acquisition and resettlement costs, together with lower bids, produced US$4.6 million of savings in mid-2018 that were reallocated to other activities. The completion report of 23 February 2021 and the Independent Evaluation Group's review both rate the overall outcome Satisfactory on a split rating.
case.killed_note: One death: a crane operator killed when the crane fell over at a project road construction site. The completion report's cause analysis places the accident during the unloading of steel bars from a truck, and the report adds that the Bank did not consider it non-compliance because adequate environmental safeguards had been established for the project. Neither the completion report nor the Evaluation Group's review attributes the death to a named failure of site safety management.

case.title: Guaraqueçaba Carbon Reserves and the Green Police
case.point: Antonina, where Antonio Alves was jailed, beside the Cachoeira reserve (approximate)

lenders.name: General Motors, Chevron and American Electric Power (companies paying for carbon rights)
lenders.role: US companies, not grant-makers. They gave $18 million through The Nature Conservancy to buy about 50,000 acres: GM $10 million for Cachoeira, AEP $5 million for Serra do Itaqui, Chevron $3 million for Morro da Mina, to offset their emissions (Mother Jones). Ecosystem Marketplace gives AEP $5.4 million.

lenders.name: The Nature Conservancy
lenders.role: Led the project with the companies' money; its Brazilian partner SPVS manages the reserves.

case.conditions: Land was bought from 2000 and closed to use so that the carbon in its trees could be credited to the funding companies. SPVS trained the state Green Police (Força Verde), who patrol the reserves (Mother Jones).
case.community: Antonio Alves, 35, spent 11 days in jail in Antonina for cutting a tree to repair his mother's home in Quara Quara; three of its five cabins stood empty, and he said people left because they could no longer hunt and gather. Farmer Jonas de Souza said he could no longer hunt, fish or gather palm hearts. Antonina's mayor said he had defended several villagers charged under reserve rules (Mother Jones). SPVS first hired 47 local people and later let most go; seven remained, and a woman said officers handcuffed her husband at home (World Rainforest Movement).
case.suppression: Residents say officers entered homes without proper authorisation, sometimes armed, and seized knives and other items (World Rainforest Movement).
case.ecosystem: Atlantic forest, of which only 7% remains (Mother Jones).
case.outcome: TNC said income programmes like beekeeping and organic bananas ended because the money ran out. Since 2003, 20 families have lived on land they occupied with the landless workers' movement MST (World Rainforest Movement).
